newsitem.title: USA: Supreme Court to hear Clinton sex-harassment case.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court to hear Clinton sex-harassment case.

text.p: On Monday, as President Bill Clinton should be relishing plans for his inaugural galas and brainstorming second-term policy initiatives, he will get a cold dose of controversy.

That morning, the U.S. Supreme Court is to hear arguments on whether a sexual harassment suit by Paula Jones, a woman from Arkansas, should be allowed to proceed while Clinton is still president or deferred until he leaves the White House.
It is a suit whose allegations, already publicly detailed by Jones, not only revive recollections of Clinton's onetime reputation as a philanderer but are steamy and shocking in their own right.
That detail does not concern the high court, which had loftier matters in mind when it agreed to hear the dispute.
It will consider for the first time, during the hour-long arguments, whether a sitting president may be sued for damages for events that happened before he took office.

The nine justices will focus on when Jones's lawsuit can go forward -- not the merits of her allegations that Clinton made unwanted advances in 1991 in a Little Rock hotel room when he was governor of Arkansas and she was a state employee.
She seeks $700,000 in damages.
A ruling is due by the end of the court's term in June.
If it rules against Clinton, a federal judge could require him to submit to pre-trial questioning and then a trial in Arkansas, where the case has been pending since 1994.
White House officials said Clinton, who has denied the allegations, has no plans to attend the arguments, scheduled just a week before his Jan. 20 inauguration.

Asked if the hearing would be an unwelcome distraction, he said on Friday, "I don't have any control over what anyone else does; I can only control what I do. It's not going to cause me any difficulty because I'm going to do my job here."

Joseph Cammarata, an attorney for Jones, said his client, who now lives in California, would not be present to hear the momentous arguments either, mainly out of concern her presence could spark a "media spectacle" afterwards.

"She is confident her good name and reputation will be restored," Cammarata said. "There is no support in the Constitution for the relief the president seeks. We don't have a nation of kings. We have a nation of public servants. No one is above the law."
Texas Tech University law professor Thomas Baker described the case as more important politically than from a constitutional law standpoint.

"And politically, it is ironic that the issue that was everything is the issue the parties are still fighting over -- timing," he said in an analysis for an American Bar Association publication on Supreme Court cases.

In written arguments submitted to the high court, Clinton's attorney, Robert Bennett, said civil lawsuits against a sitting president must be delayed because they would be "burdensome and disruptive," distracting him from the duties of the job.
He said no president in U.S. history has ever been required to give evidence in a civil proceeding, much less appear as a defendant in court.
Bennett refused comment on the case.
"Since I will be arguing the president's case before the Supreme Court on January 13, I believe this is a time to be circumspect," he said.
The Justice Department under Attorney General Janet Reno has supported Clinton's arguments for a delay.
Reno said the Justice Department was not proposing complete presidential immunity for all civil lawsuits.
"But considering the tremendous burdens on the president, the matter should be delayed until after the service of the president," she told reporters recently.
A group of 16 law professors also submitted a court brief in support of Clinton while the American Civil Liberties Union and a group of nine law professors backed Jones's position.

There have been unsuccessful efforts to settle the case out of court, once before it was filed and again in June before the Supreme Court decided to hear Clinton's appeal that the lawsuit should be delayed, lawyers familiar with the talks have said.
